article_blocks.text: Strain Type: Indica-dominant hybrid
Genetics: Unknown three-way hybrid
Breeder: Krome / legacy Florida clone-only selection
THC Content: 20%–30%
CBD Content: Generally very low
Terpene Profile: Myrcene , Caryophyllene , Limonene
Primary Flavors: Pine, earth, wood, mild herbs, hashy spice
Flowering Time (Indoor): Approximately 58–63 days
Outdoor Harvest Time: Early to mid-October
Indoor Yield: 450–550 g/m²
Outdoor Yield: Moderate to heavy
Grow Difficulty: Moderate

Few cannabis cultivars have built such a large reputation while smelling so comparatively quiet. The White became famous not because it filled a room with fruit, fuel, or skunk, but because mature flowers could appear almost buried beneath trichomes. Under strong light, properly grown buds take on a pale, powdered appearance that explains the name immediately. That resin production helped turn an obscure Florida clone into prized breeding material, eventually placing its genetics behind scores of later marijuana hybrids. The effects are equally serious: an initially balanced head-and-body sensation can accumulate into substantial relaxation, while the subdued pine, earth, and woody flavor stands in sharp contrast to the intensely aromatic dessert weed that dominates the modern market.
Genetics and Lineage

The White’s history has accumulated plenty of misinformation. Most importantly, it has no documented connection to White Widow . The name came strictly from the finished buds looking as though they had been coated in confectioners’ sugar. Krome also identified the plant’s earlier name as Triangle and described it as a three-way cross, while distinguishing it specifically from the separate Florida cultivar Triangle Kush . Its three actual parental strains were never publicly established.

Modern genetic preservation efforts support that cautious interpretation. HENDRX, which maintains a preserved cut in its cannabis library , lists The White—also called The Triangle—as an unknown hybrid and explicitly warns that historical stories often confuse it with Triangle Kush even though the plants express differently. HENDRX traces its particular preserved clone through a holder who had maintained the cut since at least 2009. The cultivar is a mostly indica, clone-only strain and notes that it took second place in the indica growers category at the 2009 IC 420 Growers Cup.

Its breeding legacy is much easier to document than its ancestry. There are more than 180 direct descendants involving The White, illustrating how extensively breeders have used the clone to increase resin, potency, flower density, and visual appeal in later hybrids. The mysterious pedigree therefore became less important over time than the traits the plant reliably passed forward.
Effects and Experience

The first phase can feel remarkably even. Instead of launching immediately into either racy cerebral stimulation or overwhelming body heaviness, the experience often establishes itself across both mind and body. A mild euphoric shift may make conversation, music, television, or quiet hobbies more enjoyable while physical tension begins to recede in the background. Relaxation, sleepiness, and euphoria are among the cultivar’s most frequently reported effects.

Relaxation usually becomes more influential as time passes. Muscles feel heavier, movement becomes less appealing, and the mental component turns quieter without necessarily disappearing. At moderate amounts, experienced consumers may still enjoy an unhurried social evening or movie. Larger servings can move much closer to couch-lock territory, with lowered motivation and drowsiness becoming increasingly prominent. This makes the strain better suited to late-day cannabis use than activities requiring sustained coordination or concentration.
Medical Benefits

For medical marijuana consumers, the attraction generally centers on physical calm and the ability to disengage from stress. The balanced opening may allow some people to remain mentally comfortable while tension gradually becomes less noticeable, whereas the heavier later phase can make persistent aches or physical restlessness easier to tolerate. User-generated data most frequently associates the cultivar with stress, pain, and anxiety, while sleepiness is among its commonly reported effects.

Evening consumption may therefore be more practical than daytime use for patients who become strongly sedated by THC. Someone whose sleep is disturbed by discomfort or mental tension may prefer the gradual progression toward heaviness, although individual response can vary dramatically. A person sensitive to THC may experience the opposite of relaxation if the dose is excessive, particularly when flower approaches the upper end of the potency range.

There are no controlled clinical studies showing that The White specifically treats insomnia, chronic pain, anxiety, or another disorder. Research on cannabis more broadly suggests that some THC/CBD-containing preparations may reduce chronic pain in the short term, but adverse effects such as dizziness and sleepiness can occur, and evidence for anxiety remains limited. Medical consumers should therefore treat strain descriptions as reference information rather than proof of therapeutic effectiveness.
Flavor Profile and Aroma

Here, understatement is part of the identity. The White became legendary during an era when powerful cannabis was often expected to announce itself with skunk, Kush, or fuel, yet this clone can produce an unexpectedly restrained scent. The aroma and flavor is unusually mild compared with similarly potent OG-type flower , with pine, earth, and wood among the most frequently identified flavors. HENDRX likewise characterizes the preserved cultivar as having a muted, nostalgic aroma rather than the obvious gas associated with Triangle Kush.

Laboratory data gives the quieter profile more context. Myrcene can reinforce earthy and herbal depth, caryophyllene adds dry peppery spice, and limonene provides a lighter citrus edge. The overall impression, however, remains far less flamboyant than most contemporary fruit or candy hybrids.

The inhale commonly favors dry earth, soft pine, herbs, and wood rather than syrupy sweetness. Hash-like spice may become clearer on the exhale, sometimes accompanied by faint citrus or pepper. For terpene hunters accustomed to loud Gelato or Zkittlez descendants, the restrained flavor can seem almost strange. Yet that contrast is part of the cultivar’s character: exceptionally frosted marijuana does not necessarily have to produce an equally aggressive aroma.
Growing Information

The White’s most valuable cultivation trait is impossible to miss once flowering advances. Trichome coverage develops heavily across the buds and nearby leaves, eventually giving mature flowers the frosted appearance responsible for the cultivar’s name. The White has an indoor finishing window of approximately 58–63 days, early-to-mid-October outdoor maturity, medium height, upright vertical growth, fast development, and moderate-to-heavy yield potential.

The plant responds well to canopy management. It takes well to topping and reports indoor production around 450–550 grams per square meter, while the cultivar is responsive to relatively strong feeding programs. Topping before flowering can divide vertical growth between several productive branches, and low-stress training helps spread those sites across the available light. Support may become necessary as mature resin-heavy flowers accumulate weight.

Late flowering calls for disciplined humidity control because dense cannabis buds can hold moisture around their interior calyxes. Consistent airflow and a clean, uncrowded canopy help reduce problems as harvest approaches. Growers working with the authentic clone should also remember that seed products carrying the same name may be selfed reproductions or hybrids rather than the original genotype. Preservation through cloning remains the clearest way to maintain the specific plant that made The White famous.
FAQ
What are the genetics of The White?
Its exact parentage is unknown. Krome described the original plant as a three-way cross called Triangle, but the identities of those three parents have never been reliably documented.
Is The White related to White Widow?

No verified connection exists. Krome specifically stated that The White had no known relationship to White Widow and explained that its name refers to the exceptionally pale, trichome-covered appearance of mature buds.
Is The White the same strain as Triangle Kush?

No. Historical confusion exists because The White was originally called Triangle, but Krome distinguished it from the separate Triangle Kush cultivar. Modern preservation sources also treat the two as different plants.
How strong is The White?
Potency depends on cultivation and batch.
How long does The White take to flower?
Approximately eight to nine weeks is typical. HENDRX records 58–63 days indoors. Outdoor plants generally reach maturity in early to mid-October under suitable conditions.
Final Thoughts on The White

The White occupies an unusual position in cannabis history. Its parents remain unidentified, its aroma is understated, and even its original Triangle name has caused decades of confusion with another famous Florida cultivar. Yet the plant required none of those details to become influential. Extraordinary trichome production, substantial potency, dependable relaxation, and strong breeding value were enough to carry the clone far beyond the Florida circle in which it first circulated. Its second-place finish at the 2009 IC 420 Growers Cup and extensive list of descendants reflect that lasting genetic reputation.

Modern cannabis increasingly competes through louder fruit, candy, and fuel profiles, which makes this cultivar feel almost countercultural today. The buds can look spectacular while smelling surprisingly restrained; the high can begin balanced before gradually becoming heavy; and the genetics remain mysterious despite their influence on generations of breeding. For consumers interested in classic clone-only weed and growers fascinated by resin production, The White remains a distinctive piece of American cannabis history—and proof that a plant does not need a famous pedigree to leave one behind.
